reviews.author: YennaPPa (Luscious.K)
reviews.text:
#Cheongdam-dong #Byeokje Galbi the Cheongdam Part 1

“K-BBQ fine dining from the top Byeokje Galbi brand”

Among Korea's Korean beef restaurants, the two that have traditionally had the most famous names would probably be Wah.

Byeokje Galbi has already made efforts to brand itself and has already succeeded in creating an outstanding brand, and Bongpiyang's cold noodles have a popularity and recognition that surpasses that of Byeokje Galbi.
However, this expansion also had its ups and downs, including the dismal failure of Cheongmisim, which launched in Cheongdam-dong as a high-end brand combining Byeokje Galbi and Bongpiyang.

Based on that experience, Byeokje Galbi's top high-end brand was launched in the former Cheongmisim space by adding the brand power of Byeokje Galbi, the purchasing power of the highest quality Korean beef, and Saju's interest in seafood.

It is composed of all seating rooms, so you can enjoy private yet luxurious grilled Korean beef. Reflecting the popularity of omakase of the time, not only is it offering a 250,000 won entree menu, but it also offers a charcoal-grilled format for people like me who don't like entrusted Korean beef, so you can enjoy a wide range of fine dining at Byeokje Galbi.

There are a variety of table settings for lunch, so there are also lunch options that allow you to entertain in a luxurious manner.

Positioned as a high-end restaurant available in all weathers in Cheongdam-dong... but the prices are not cheap.

Although Byeokje Galbi is a very expensive restaurant, this place offers Korean beef of a higher standard and the service and prices are set accordingly. This restaurant's signature flower bone raw ribs are sold by the bone unit, usually weighing around 1kg-1.5kg and priced at 65,000 won per 100g, so if 4 adults visit and order 1.5kg, the basic price is about 1 million won.
Sulwha Korean beef raw ribs cost 80,000 won per 100g, so it is not a price you can comfortably eat anyway.

However, that doesn't mean it's just expensive. The atmosphere is similar to Cheongmisim, but I like the simple yet more luxurious exterior and interior. The indoor room atmosphere is clean and odor-free. In particular, the ceramics used are designed and custom-made by the chairman's wife, who is very interested in ceramics, so they are rare and can only be enjoyed here, giving the Korean restaurant a more luxurious feel.

Unlike Byeokje Galbi, where the grilling service was not much different compared to the high price, the aunts seem to have received special training and provide much more veteran and comfortable service, and their grilling skills are also good. In particular, when ordering raw kkotbone ribs, one of the attractions is the performance in which the diamond cut sheath developed by Byeokje Galbi is demonstrated and shaped in front of your eyes.

The disciple of the person who developed the diamond sheath for the first time in Korea (the teacher is in charge of omakase) goes around the room demonstrating it and also gives a brief explanation about the meat. In addition, they are meticulous in making up for the loss due to the removal of fat and connective tissue that occurs when preparing meat with other meat, which helps control the hearts of customers who pay a high price.

I felt like I was being treated a little better as I was given a special piece of meat to compensate for the loss from the 1.3kg ribs I had ordered. The side dishes and pre-dinner dishes are also really good.

Unlike when they only served meat, they gave me 4 kinds of appetizers that served as an amuse before the meal, and they gave me a piece of well-ripened grouper and sea bream each for a quick meal, so I felt good right from the start.

The quality of the side dishes and conditioning was impressively good, so there were no complaints about the taste throughout the meal. He never felt like it was a waste of money.

PS: The reason I like the format of this restaurant is because of the façade of the Korean beef omakase format. Omakase is a given at sushi restaurants. There can be hundreds of basic seafood ingredients if you like, and various techniques can be applied to them depending on the chef's abilities.
But is this possible with Korean beef?
No matter how much you subdivide the parts, there will be about 20 to 30 types, and among them, there are no techniques that can be applied much other than grilling and sashimi.
The Korean beef omakase, which costs more than 200,000 won per person for a few small dishes and a few pieces of meat, is not my taste, no matter how I look at it.
In conclusion, I spent the same amount of money at this restaurant, but I ate ribs and other top quality Korean beef to the point where I was full. I didn't feel like I was hungry after eating at fine dining.
Willing to visit again?
Of course there is.
Rather than coming out hungry after eating a few unidentified dishes and pieces of meat at a Korean beef omakase, it is better to eat a lot of Korean 0.1% Korean beef at a similar price here.

reviews.author: ANNEZUE
reviews.text:
The owner is friendly and nice. I visited for a walk-in lunch and there were about 2 people waiting, so I sat down and waited.
I ordered gomtang set meal A (half plate of gomtang + grilled seasoned meat), gomtang set meal B (half plate of gomtang + octopus carpaccio), additional toppings such as pollack roe, seasoned fan meat suji, roasted sweet potato cream brûlée & heart sweet red bean.
The gomtang soup is rich, clear, and seasoned just right. It's delicious.
The seasoned grill was also very delicious. It was grilled with a torch, so it had a fiery scent. The pollack roe mayo and crab sauce were salty and flavorful, and went well with the meat and chives.
The octopus carpaccio had jelly stuck between the slices of octopus. It had a subtle taste and a subtle refreshing scent. It was edible when eaten with lemon, but it was difficult to tell what it tasted like and it wasn't very good. I don't think I'll eat it a second time.
The seasoned suji was a neat seasoned meat, but it was disappointing that the added sauce and flavor were underwhelming. I think it is correct to say that it was mild. The taste of the gomtang was clear. It was seasoned well and the seasoned grilled set meal was the most delicious among the side dishes.
The roasted sweet potato cream brûlée I ordered for dessert was the worst. The crumbly and chewy roasted sweet potatoes were topped with rock-like ice cream that looked like BB Big Ice Cream. Sweet potatoes turn sour when they get old, but the sweet potatoes they served had a strong sour taste. The ice cream was so frozen that it didn't go well with the sweet potatoes or taste good. It was more like an ice cookie with red bean granules in it. I think a scoop of milk or vanilla ice cream would have been better. Since it was called sweet potato creme brûlée, I thought it would be a creme brûlée made with sweet potatoes. It would have been nice if the sweet potatoes were sweet and fresh without being sour. At the end, they gave me citron and grapefruit tea, which I enjoyed.
I'm full, but I don't think I'll come back a second time because it's disappointing and inconvenient.

reviews.text:
I went to Lee Wonil Table, a Korean restaurant run by famous chef Lee Wonil. I visited without a reservation for lunch on a weekday.

I liked the overall clean and luxurious atmosphere of a Korean restaurant, from the entrance to the interior.

Two people ordered seafood kimchi pancake (16,000 won), grilled pork belly with red pepper paste (32,000 won), and soy sauce crab sauce (38,000 won).

The seafood kimchi pancake didn't have a very special taste; rather, it felt like the kimchi pancake we're familiar with made really well. It was crispy yet chewy and had plenty of shrimp and squid, so I was satisfied.

Grilled pork belly with red pepper paste was also quite delicious. The red pepper paste seasoning was not too heavy and had a nice balance of sweetness and subtle spiciness, and the meat was grilled very well. I especially liked the seasoned cabbage sprouts that came with it. The whole perilla seeds were savory yet balanced out the rich flavor of the pork belly, making it a perfect match.

The soy sauce crab sauce was so delicious that I forgot to take a picture. It was a female crab full of eggs and felt fresh. Even though I was already full, I quickly finished my bowl of rice because the soy sauce was so good.

Luckily, Chef Wonil Lee came by during the meal and said he would take a picture with me first, so I was grateful. (I'm not sure how often you come to the restaurant)

The staff were overall very friendly and explained the menu well.

Oh, by the way, the fact that it's corkage free is also an advantage. However, the lineup of Korean alcohol sold in the store looks good, so it might be a good idea to try some recommended drinks at the store along with food.

Overall, it was a very satisfactory meal, except that the location was a bit difficult to access by public transportation.

reviews.author: ethan ghymn
reviews.text:
On the way back from taking my young family member to school in the morning, my family member asked to buy some kimbap from Gangnam Kimbab. I wondered if there were any other kimbap stores other than Gangnam Kimbab. When I pulled out Naver Maps, I couldn't see anything other than chain stores or stores I'd already been to. I've heard the name of Kimbab Heaven many times, but I don't remember actually eating kimbap, so I decided to stop by.

I called to order in advance and asked about the popular kimbap menu, and they said king sausage kimbap. I tried king sausage kimbap before at a local Food 2900 Nonhyeon City branch, so when I inquired about other kimbap menus, they said tuna kimbap was also consistently popular, so I asked for the basic kimbap, one plain kimbap and one tuna kimbap each.

When we arrived quickly, they were diligently rolling up the kimbap and handing it to us in a plastic bag wrapped in aluminum foil.

When I brought it home, a family member asked why I didn't buy it at Gangnam Gimbap, so I said I'd buy it at Gangnam Gimbap next time, and when I unpacked it, I didn't know if it was the original, but the regular kimbap seemed a bit lacking in volume compared to the tuna kimbap, and when I tasted each piece, the overall balance was okay, but it tasted too old-fashioned, so I compared it to the Namdaemun plump kimbap last time.

Overall, I've heard the name a lot, but I don't remember actually stopping by and tasting kimbap. I stopped by and got takeout and tried plain kimbap and tuna kimbap. It wasn't bad, but I vaguely remember the price, so I thought it was cheaper, but with prices going up these days, it doesn't feel that cheap, and more than anything, it tastes too old-fashioned, so I don't think I'll visit again, but the overall balance wasn't bad, so it's okay.

reviews.text:
#Cheongdam-dong #Rovata Livera

“Great food, better service, but disappointing liquor policy”

Is it 2017? A second robatayaki boom occurred in Korea with the emergence of a restaurant in Apgujeong-dong that roasted chicken in front of customers in an innovative way that went beyond the concept of a few restaurants that had maintained the reputation of robatayaki in the past.

Since then, many more stores have opened as if it were a trend, and in 2019, a store was created that serves this type of cuisine. Stores that always open following trends tend to go through natural selection, but Live here remains a popular store thanks to its solid cooking skills and original Instagrammable concept.

 Honestly, this is a strange term I’m hearing for the first time. But it's not to the point where you don't know what I'm talking about, and it's a primitive method of wood-fired grilling? It is a fairly intuitive word that is easily understood. Looking at the picture, it was not a direct fire, but a method of grilling from the side using the heat of a charcoal fire. This is a grilling method that brings back memories of my mother putting mackerel on a bamboo needle, sprinkling a lot of coarse salt on it, and then roasting it over a bonfire, when I was in elementary school a few decades ago and would set up a tent and play camping in the yard of my house. The taste is truly amazing, and even though it was mackerel I bought at the market, the taste of biting into the mackerel, grilled fragrantly without any fishy smell due to the wood fire, is still imprinted in my mind. Therefore, this house was a place that stimulated my original memories, and I really wanted to visit it at least once.

The store is smaller than expected. It consists of tachi seats that can seat up to 10 people, and the scene of seafood and vegetables being taken out and cooked in an ice showcase where fresh seafood is displayed is similar to any other robatayaki setting. However, the original grilling brazier inside the store catches the eye.

Among binchotan charcoals that look sturdy at first glance, only long charcoals are used to ignite the fire well and maintain the fire. The food ingredients are grilled next to the charcoal. Since the heat from the binchotan charcoal is received from the side rather than from below, the intense heat is gradually transferred to the ingredients, creating the perfect conditions for grilling. It can be said to be a healthy grilling method that allows grilling without soot because the oil dripping from the ingredients does not directly touch the fire. The downside is of course the long cooking time. Instead, for those who can sublimate this boring shortcoming into enjoyment, it can be said that this is a place where basic taste is guaranteed.

In addition to the signature course, I asked for futomaki, grilled vegetables, grilled rockfish, grilled chicken, and grilled eel, and as the drinkers drank, they provided various snacks as a service.

The food here is largely divided into sashimi, grilled raw fish, robatayaki, and soup, and the overall quality of the food is excellent regardless of the genre. A lot of effort was made to maintain the taste of the ingredients as much as possible, so the seasoning of the food was light and appropriate, and excessive decoration was excluded, so I was more satisfied than I had feared.Sashimi, mackerel sushi, and futomaki are better than average for a Japanese restaurant. The ingredients were fresh and the level of aging was good, but the mackerel sushi served was a testament to the restaurant's skill in shime. I am not a professional sushi chef, so even though the shape is a bit messed up, the taste is guaranteed. Futomaki also achieved good balance at a level that was not too burdensome.

The grilled raw fish, which is this restaurant's specialty, was delicious, but it didn't meet my expectations. Geumtae, which was moist and well-grilled, was delicious with the savory flavor of the fat and the lightness of the white meat, and the rockfish, which becomes a bit dry when grilled, was grilled raw and finished with a very light grill. What can I say about grilled chicken legs... However, the dryness of the skin (we call this outer skin) felt when grilled using charcoal or grilled over a campfire as I know it, was less than expected, so I think it didn't reach the level of skin texture I expected. For personal preference, wouldn’t it be okay to bake it a little longer?

The cooking skills of this restaurant are evident in the scallops given to start the grilled course. The final touch of truffle was added to the cool, not tough, grilled scallops. Very delicious. Rice is mixed with the remaining broth and served as risotto, making a great appetizer.

The other charcoal grilled items were also excellent, and the grilled vegetables were perfect, while the eel felt ordinary, perhaps due to its size. The Tsukune served instead was very delicious.

I can't help but discuss the service at this restaurant. The chef serves customers quietly but properly.
After hearing from a member of our group who had forgotten to put the shrimp tail he ate on the back of the sashimi and was laughing because he thought the chef had given him two shrimp, the service offered one shrimp on top. He had the sense to change all the foods containing truffles for people in his group who couldn't even smell the scent of truffles.
I am very impressed by the gentle response that balances cooking and conversation without losing focus on one's duties despite various offers of alcohol.

It was a very satisfying visit.
To be honest, I thought it was a concept restaurant that was taking advantage of the robatayaki trend and targeting Instagrammers with an unfamiliar weapon called raw yaki. However, the cooking skills are better than expected and the basics of grilling are solid. Even the hospitality is excellent, so you can't help but enjoy eating and drinking at this place.

However, the alcohol policy is not applicable to drinkers like me, but may be disappointing to others...
It seems that there was a recent change from originally requiring alcoholic beverages to requiring one bottle of alcohol. Two couples who had made reservations on the day of their visit just left because of the bottle order policy. It's a popular place, so it fills up right away, but it would already be a big disappointment if the customers who came with high expectations had to give up and turn away because of the alcohol policy.
I think this part needs to be properly conveyed through notifications.

Thank you, Chef, for creating a fun dinner...

“Space and visual values”

A large Japanese restaurant suddenly opened at the southern end of Yeongdong Bridge.

I heard that it wasn't bad for a cost-effective lunch course.

Even the name

reviews.author: ethan ghymn
reviews.text:
Since my family was gone and I was home alone, I took out the map to see if there was a place I wanted to go for dinner near my house, and I saw Sugitama, a Namazake bar on the first floor of the building where Katsuro, where I used to occasionally stop by and eat tonkatsu before the premium tonkatsu stores near my house that I saved in my want to go list after reading Kkomo's review, caught my eye.

I don't really enjoy alcohol, but when I went to this store's Instagram account, I saw that they had posted on the feed that they were holding an event on Christmas Eve and Christmas Day where you could try a special Christmas set of 6 types of sake from Yamaguchi for 10,000 won. I like events, and I happened to be alone today, so I walked out of my house to taste it, and it was close to my house, so I arrived quickly.

I like beer and wine, and I have a body where just the smell of shochu makes me vomit, so I was curious about what it would be like to specialize in namazake, which is not wine but has the taste of Japanese wine, and namazake, which is not heat-treated.

When I arrived in front of the store a little after 7 o'clock, I thought it would be crowded, but I don't know if it was because I've never been to a bar like this before or because it was still early, but there was only one person sitting at the bar, and when I went in, he got up and said he was the owner.

As I sat down, I told him that it was my first time coming to a place like this, and he told me about the Christmas special 6-type sake set event. I asked if there were any fried foods like aji frai (fried horse mackerel) or kaki frai (fried oysters) for snacks. When I looked at the menu written on the wall, I couldn't see any fried foods in particular, so I was worried. He said I could order from Katsuro's menu on the upper floor. I asked him if he was the son of Mr. and Mrs. Katsuro, and he said yes. He said, “Aha, that’s right.”

It would have been good in the past, but these days, there are so many good tonkatsu restaurants that I want to try the side dishes prepared here rather than ordering from Katsurou. The owner said that the most popular menu item is braised radish, but if you are looking for something with a meaty feel, the gyusuji nikomi, which is simmered beef tendon and radish together, is good. I'm still an elementary school student, but I also have the taste of a princess, so I haven't tried anything like suji, but I think I'll try it as an adult. Please give me Nikomi.

The owner first served us a salty, savory, and umami-tasting snack mixed with salted orchids and nuts such as sunflower seeds, then prepared 6 small plastic tasting cups, took out 6 types of sake from the refrigerator, and began to pour wine in the order written on the menu. He poured each of the 6 types of sake while explaining them one by one so that the small tasting cup would not overflow, and the sake label was visible for a moment. After putting it in the refrigerator, he took out the Kyusuji Nikomi, warmed it up, and placed it in front of him.

He said that it is recommended to eat the regular braised radish cold, which has a cleaner feel, and to eat the Kyusuji Nikomi warm.

Namazake is a sake that has not been heat-treated. To put it simply, you can think of it as the difference in taste between low-temperature-treated Pasteur milk and regular milk.

When I tasted them in order, the first Choyofuku Musume Chokaraguchi Jikagumi had what I thought was a standard taste of typical sake, and the second one had a bright and pleasant aroma without the stickiness at all. The teacher explained that this was the characteristic aroma of sake brewed from rice called Yamada Nishiki at a sake brewery in Yamaguchi Prefecture.When I first tasted the braised radish in the gyusuji nikomi in front of me, it was sweet and soft, and the taste was similar to the taste and feel of the braised ribs that my mother makes on holidays such as Lunar New Year and Chuseok. Next, I mustered up the courage to taste the gyusuji, and it was so soft and chewy that it felt like eating konjac, so I guess I must have eaten it a long time ago.

I tried to drink several types of namazake, rinsing my mouth with water in between, and drinking them all, but each tasted slightly different. Perhaps because it was my first namazake experience, only the first namazake felt standard, and the rest of the namazake felt slightly different, but I got the impression that they all had the characteristic of a bright scent to some extent, even though they were made using the same Yamadanishiki rice.

This time, I told him that I wanted to try a different flavor of namazake, and he asked me which one I liked, and I wasn't sure, but I said that the second and fourth ones were good. He asked me if I liked wine, and I answered yes. Then, he told me to try the wine-like namazake, and poured an overflowing bottle of Sensational Black Origaramiran namazake, which also tastes like wine, into a coaster, explaining that it feels different to drink it from a cup than from a wide coaster. Referee.

When I first tasted what was poured in the cup, I thought it was strange because it had the scent of sake but really felt like wine. When I told him that I liked it, he said that this namazake was a limited edition, so once the bottle sold out, I wouldn't be able to taste the same thing again.

I was curious about other snacks and asked, and he said that cream cheese and shoto are the most basic and popular menu items found in most Japanese sake bars. Please explain that shoto means alcohol thief.

He placed it in front of me and explained that if you scoop up a small amount of chouto, a salted fish made from tuna intestines, with chopsticks and taste it, scoop up cream cheese and taste it before it disappears in your mouth, and drink namazake before it disappears in your mouth, the flavor will explode.

First, I scooped up the chouto with chopsticks and tasted it. I really like the salty taste of the scallion salt that you eat when you go to Jeju Island, and it had that kind of salty taste, so I immediately liked it. Just as I heard in the explanation, I put the cream cheese in my mouth before the shoto disappeared in my mouth. As expected, I could immediately feel that it was very salty and went well with the taste of the cream cheese. As expected, I drank the sensational black origalami before the shoto and cream cheese disappeared. It felt like the umami was really exploding in my mouth, and I couldn't help but nod why I love mariage and why it is such a popular snack.

Kyusuji Nikomi has a sweet taste like braised ribs, so it's delicious to eat on its own, but the salty cream cheese and shuto mariage is much better to eat with sake as a snack.

The owner said that the sake has a tap water of about 16-20 degrees, which is higher than soju, so it is soft but has a high tap. Around this time, I felt my lower stomach becoming warm, and a young female customer dressed as a rider, who must have been riding a motorcycle, came in and was talking to the owner as if she was a regular customer. When I asked him when he started this sake bar, he said it was in October of last year, not 8 types of namazake, but 8 bottles. It's been about a year and two months since I started, and now there are over 200 types.

It felt like my first experience with not only namazake, but also sake itself, so I got up and paid at this point, and they said it was 30,000 won. I don't drink a lot, so I didn't drink much. Since there was a Christmas event, the price felt relatively cheap, and it was a new and good experience, so it was a pleasant visit and I thought I might stop by again. As I was leaving, I saw another team of male and female customers coming in, and I thought this was the beginning.

reviews.text:
It's delicious, but I feel like it's a waste since I spent over 360,000 won per person.

To be honest, based on the taste alone, I would give it 5 stars.
The quality of the dishes was high, and the appetizers and seafood courses in particular were neat and delicate. However, for me personally, the problem was factors other than taste.

Disappointment in customer service
We were seated according to our reservation time, but the start of the meal was delayed by more than 10 minutes.
The delay itself is understandable. However, it was disappointing that there was not even the slightest guidance on it. I ordered a draft beer, drank it, and waited.

When it comes to a Michelin 1-star restaurant, you expect not only the quality of the food but also the density and detail of the service, but this was not met. The reception wasn't rude, but it didn't feel attentive either.

Satisfaction compared to price
The food is delicious.
However, considering the price, I thought it was ordinary or a bit disappointing.

Recently, the level of kaiseki restaurants and fine dining in Seoul has risen significantly.
In such a competitive environment, the impression is that Mooney has raised the standards of those around it rather than being particularly lagging behind.

In particular, I felt that the impact of seasonal ingredients that strongly represent this season was lacking throughout the course.
The taste was decent, but the strong message of seasonality that could persuade the price was somewhat weak.

Sake Pairing
We also had sake pairing, but it was a bit disappointing.
The grade wasn't high, and it was more of a setup that allowed you to experience different types of sake rather than an elaborate match to the menu.
Compared to the delicacy of the dish, the design of the pairing felt somewhat flat.

Space & Atmosphere
It leaves the impression that the space is a bit outdated.
Perhaps because the kaiseki and fine dining spaces competing these days are so excellent, it felt a bit disappointing in comparison. a little messy

reviews.author: ethan ghymn
reviews.text:
I went to Mitas Cheongdam's Lunch Sushi Omakase on Sugitama's Instagram, which is a Namazake Bar that I visited last time. I heard that it has an incredible price of 45,000 won and that it has excellent composition and taste, so I thought it would be worth stopping by once if the owner of Sugitama said it was good, so I saved it as I wanted to go.

Looking here and there, I saw that Mitasu, an izakaya in Ichon-dong, had opened a new restaurant in Cheongdam-dong. Kikuga in Ichon-dong used to be famous for its sushi, but to me, Ichon-dong is called Little Tokyo because so many Japanese people live here that there are many restaurants that serve pretty good Japanese food. As a person who likes Japanese food, I often went to this neighborhood, so I had the image of being able to taste delicious Japanese food rather than sushi, so I probably wouldn't have liked it if I hadn't said it was good on Sugitama's Instagram. I feel like I wouldn't be attracted to it.

I heard that the lunch omakase is only available until June, so I wanted to stop by quickly before the end of June, so I called the store and at first they said they had no vacancies this week, but I guess they checked again and there were cancellations, so they said there were seats, so I made a reservation and stopped by for lunch today.

I walked because it was close to my house, and it was located near the old JYP practice room. I arrived a little early through the external stairs leading directly to the second floor. I was a little early, but when I asked if I could go in, they told me to come in, so I went in. The store had counter seats and a couple of rooms. After checking the name of the person who made the reservation, I sat in the counter seat that was shown to me.

There was a lot of sake on display at the back of Izakaya Yeosenji, and the saleswoman, who seemed to be quick-witted, asked if I would like hot tea or cold tea. I asked for cold tea.

The female clerk brought me cold tea and asked how I knew about it. I was about to say 500 won, but I told her that I found out about it after seeing it on Sugitama's Instagram.

They also brought me a menu and a sake menu, but I didn't really have any thoughts on alcohol, so I just took a picture and put it down, but there were so many sake menus that I didn't take a picture.

When I asked when they opened, they said they opened in September last year. When I asked if they were only offering lunch omakase until June, they said yes, and that it was because of the coronavirus, but now they are only open for dinner as usual.

First, chawanmushi with a generous amount of clams and clams was served. They said it would be good to season it with a generous amount of wasabi, so I ate it that way and the taste wasn't particularly special, but the generous amount of clams felt new.

Next came the steamed abalone, which was moderately soft, but relatively unimpressive. The first sushi starter was sea bream belly, tuna belly, miso soup, amberjack topped with minced garlic, tsukehan tuna flesh, benjali with the skin on, sweet shrimp, frittered tuna belly sprinkled with salt, uni from Gangwon-do, cuttlefish sprinkled with yuzu juice, frizzled herring, frizzled herring. Sea bream, mackerel stick sushi, and anagoro sushi to mark the end conclude the meal.

The sushi was good in its own way with tuna belly meat, soft tuna meat, sweet shrimp, soft tuna belly meat, and anago, but it felt like there were too many soft things, and there were some things that felt bitter because they were slightly too soft, and I wondered if they were trying to cover up the poor quality of the ash with a bad flavor rather than improving the flavor. Uni also had some sweetness, but it wasn't melty, and it was relatively soft and had an aftertaste. It was a bit disappointing, why did it come in a 45,000 won course? But as expected, the quality was disappointing.

Torishiomen was served for the meal. The noodles were somewhat reminiscent of Korean somen, but the broth had a Japanese feel, so it didn't really go well with it, but it was still clean and seasoned well, so it was good.

For dessert, they served something called blancmange. They said it tasted like pudding and that it contained ground roasted sesame seeds. When I tasted it, it had the texture of penna cotta, with the nuttiness and oiliness of ground sesame seeds. The blancmanger itself was nutty and delicious, but it didn't have a refreshing finish, which was disappointing.

I stopped by after making a quick reservation to find a place where I could enjoy lunch omakase that was overall delicious and cost-effective. It wasn't a particularly wow-inducing experience, but considering the neighborhood, I felt the cost-effectiveness was pretty good, so it's somewhere between ok and delicious, but since it's a new store, I said it was delicious to show my support.

reviews.text:
🌙 Cheongdam-dong Tsukiyowa — The essence of eel rice bowl, as soft as a moonlit night in Tokyo

🌙 Cheongdam-dong Tsukiyowa (月夜は) — A world of eel as refined as a moonlit night

Cheongdam-dong, Seoul. *Tsukiyowa (月夜は)*, a space with an elegant name, welcomes guests in a quiet, restrained atmosphere. A house that quietly brings out the essence rather than showing something. The Tokyo-style eel rice bowl served here allows you to experience the deep world of Japanese eel cuisine.

⸻

🍱 Refined Japanese style, meet the essence of eel

Tsukiyowa's eel is Tokyo-style (Kanto-style). It is different from the Nagoya style ‘Hitsumabushi’ or Kansai’s direct fire grilling that we commonly eat. The eel here is steamed once and then carefully grilled over charcoal. Through this process, the oil is removed and the texture becomes extremely soft. Although it is coated with tare (a sweet soy sauce-based sauce), the taste is subtle and understated. It's not excessive. A refined, no-frills bite shows the aesthetics of Tokyo cuisine.

⸻

🧂 Shirayaki — Focusing on the natural taste of eel

This time, for comparison, I also ordered ‘Shirayaki (白焼き)’, i.e. **grilled with salt (or grilled without seasoning)**. In this menu, the eel is grilled without any seasoning, and even salt is provided separately. If you sprinkle a little salt to suit your taste, the savory and savory taste of the eel will come to life clearly in your mouth.
Slightly crispy on the outside and soft on the inside, cooked to the perfect temperature. All that remains in your mouth is a light flavor and a clean aftertaste.

I could clearly feel the effort and consideration that went into the ingredient called eel.

⸻

🍚 The beauty of side dishes — sashimi, soup, tsugemono

The composition that came with the meal was also impressive.
The slightly fragrant bamboo shoot and mushroom soup, and **tsugemono (Japanese pickled cucumber and ginger)** filled the mouth and went well with the eel. In particular, the aged flounder and tuna sashimi were excellent in both balance and texture. There was a depth hidden in the simplicity, and it felt like a piece that completed Tsukiyowa's overall tone.

⸻

🍵 Finishing with Zarusoba — like a ray of wind

I wanted to satiate my appetite full of eel, so I ordered Zarusoba. As you can see in the photo, simple plating without any unnecessary elements. Finely chopped seaweed powder was placed on top of cold buckwheat noodles, and wasabi, daikon (ground radish), and slightly sweet **tsuyu (soba broth)** were placed side by side.

The noodles feel slightly sticky and are well-boiled and elastic. The feel of it as it passes through your mouth is cool and soft. There seems to be no better choice than this to finish off the rich flavor of eel. The unique buckwheat scent remains and does not deviate from Tsukiyowa's overall harmony.

⸻

👨‍🍳 Chef Shin Dong-hyuk — The intersection of refined techniques and Korean sensibility

Shin Dong-hyuk, the owner and chef of Tsukiyowa, is known as a chef who delicately adds Korean sensibilities and modern interpretations based on his deep understanding of Japanese cuisine in general.
He follows the traditional Japanese eel recipe, but adjusts the flavor balance and composition to naturally suit the palates of Korean customers. A tare that is not overly sweet and cooked in a comfortable way. Side dishes that are neither too salty nor too spicy.

His eel dishes speak of restrained technique and deep flavor rather than extravagance. It is closer to orthodoxy than the popular interpretation.

⸻

🌕 In conclusion

Dining at Tsukiyowa in Cheongdam-dong was an experience that was ‘subtle like moonlight but lasts a long time.’ Depth rather than stimulation, refinement rather than display.
It was at this restaurant that I realized for the first time that one ingredient, eel, has such diverse expressions and lingering emotions.

If you want a quiet flavor like a Tokyo night, a meal here will speak to you.
